articles.headline: DeepSeek Raises $15 Billion After US Agency Ban
articles.deck: Bloomberg reports funding from CATL and Tencent will support infrastructure and open models.
body: DeepSeek has raised about $15 billion two days after the United States ordered federal civilian agencies to remove its artificial intelligence technology from their systems over security concerns. Bloomberg reported the round as one of the biggest funding rounds in China. The Hangzhou based startup plans to direct the capital toward artificial intelligence infrastructure and open models for domestic and international markets. The raise proceeds despite restrictions in the United States.

Potential investors include Chinese battery maker CATL and Tencent, the company behind WeChat, among others, according to the report. The reported funding follows an investment round in June when DeepSeek raised more than $7 billion at a valuation of $50 billion. The company was also reportedly seeking an additional $1.5 billion at a valuation of around $71 billion in July. The company has plans for a potential initial public offering in China as early as next year.

The report said its expansion could further intensify competition among domestic rivals. The massive funding round is the latest sign of investors pouring billions into artificial intelligence companies around the world including those in China to compete in the global race for artificial intelligence. Kimi developer Moonshot AI secured $2 billion at a $20 billion valuation in May. Manus AI raised more than $500 million earlier this month. Chinese companies Zhipu AI and MiniMax both went public in Hong Kong in January.

Zhipu AI also known as Z.ai and MiniMax have market capitalizations of roughly $29 billion and $7.2 billion respectively as of today. DeepSeek was founded in 2023 by Liang Wenfeng who previously co founded Chinese quantitative hedge fund High Flyer which helped finance the early development of DeepSeek. The startup gained global attention in early 2025 with its free to use open weight RI reasoning model challenging the dominance of United States artificial intelligence companies. Liang retains an estimated 81.6 percent stake in its Chinese operating entity following its earlier funding round according to corporate ownership data analyzed by WireScreen.

The total of about 100 billion yuan places the transaction among the biggest funding rounds in the country. The stated focus still remains infrastructure capacity and open model development for home and foreign customers. Investor interest continues even as formal access limits remain in place for government systems in the United States.

art.caption: A modern glass office tower in Hangzhou with pedestrians on the sidewalk below. DeepSeek is based in the city and plans to direct the new capital toward infrastructure and open models.

articles.headline: Judge Rejects EPA Bid to Dismiss SpaceXAI Pollution Suit
articles.deck: Ruling preserves NAACP citizen suit over unpermitted Colossus gas turbines in Memphis.

pullquote.text: continue the fight to hold xAI accountable for the illegal air pollution it has been pumping out around the clock

body: A federal judge rejected Donald Trump’s claim that the Environmental Protection Agency can dismiss Clean Air Act citizen suits at will, keeping Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI facing a lawsuit over alleged pollution from unpermitted gas turbines at the Colossus data center in Memphis, Tennessee.

The NAACP sued after the turbines were discovered powering the giant Colossus facility. Its lawsuit sought an injunction requiring xAI, now known as SpaceXAI following a merger, to use the best available pollution control technology and ordering penalties up to $124,426 per day per violation. The group argued the turbines risked drastically spiking pollution in already vulnerable neighborhoods housing predominantly Black communities nearby.

Trump tried to intervene to block the case, arguing the EPA had power to unilaterally dismiss lawsuits any time the president decides against enforcing the Clean Air Act. He argued it would supposedly “not serve the public interest” to allow citizens to seek massive civil penalties against firms racing to build data centers to support his AI Action Plan. The judge ruled that “nothing” in the law allows the Administrator to “unilaterally dismiss a citizen suit.”

US District Judge Debra Brown called the reading an “extraordinary position” with no grounding in federal law. She wrote the power would let Trump block any lawsuit alleging data center pollution and defend any interests against Clean Air Act suits, not only the AI industry. She noted Congress allows citizens to sue the EPA administrator for failing to enforce the law, adding weight to the NAACP argument that the statute focuses on meeting standards and protecting people.

The administration pointed to a single exception allowing dismissal when the EPA is suing to require enforcement or otherwise acting to require compliance. Brown said neither applies here, where the government has made clear it has no intention to sue SpaceXAI. The NAACP argued the citizen suit is necessary for that reason. Brown agreed that cases cited by the government “arose in a context where a government acted to require abatement of unlawful pollution, not one where the government acted to shield the polluter from liability.”

Brown noted Congress considered in 1990 letting the EPA take control of citizen suits but did not adopt the change. She rejected dismissal over constitutional doubts, writing that “constitutional avoidance does not allow the Court to invent a right that does not exist in the statute.” Thoms vowed to “continue the fight to hold xAI accountable for the illegal air pollution it has been pumping out around the clock.”

articles.headline: Four-bit tables cut n-gram memory sharply
articles.deck: Tests across nanochat, Llama and GPT-2 models show preserved validation gains with lower storage.
body: Four-bit n-gram embedding tables save approximately 75 percent of table memory while preserving more than 99 percent of the validation-loss improvement from adding the tables. The finding holds across nanochat, Llama, and GPT-2 family models trained from scratch. The approach stores n-gram embeddings at low precision. The analysis tests different quantization methods and bit allocations across tables. The goal is lower memory cost with the performance gain intact. Four-bit precision is the reported balance point between savings and loss.

Many recent open-weight language models use n-gram embedding tables to improve performance. The tables store learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens. The model retrieves these representations during processing. Memory cost can be substantial. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash allocates 196 billion parameters to its Engram n-gram memory. Reduction of that cost is the central problem. Retrieval happens during processing.

Use of fewer bits leads to a larger drop in performance. A short fine-tuning phase recovers a significant part of that loss. Reinvesting the saved memory in larger tables can improve performance beyond the original full-precision tables while still using less memory. The work investigates whether memory cost can be reduced while preserving the performance improvement that the tables provide. Fewer bits mean less storage with more degradation before tuning.

Savings also extend to large existing models. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, low-bit tables save 47-55 percent of table memory. Perplexity increases by less than 1.2 percent. Downstream task performance is largely preserved. The result establishes low-bit precision as a practical way to reduce memory requirements and use saved capacity to improve model performance. The tables stay small. The gains stay. Memory saved in tables can fund larger tables for further gains. Small tables remain useful when precision stays sufficient. The margin is narrow.

articles.headline: Early AI Access Lifts Homework Not Exams
articles.deck: 153 proof students gained 2.56 points on homework with early access, while each 100 extra chatbot messages linked to a 3.02-point lower exam score.
body: 153 students in an undergraduate proof-based mathematics course received an AI chatbot and a homework-feedback interface on a staggered schedule. Students with earlier access scored 2.56 points higher on homework while only they held access. Exam performance did not differ significantly between groups. After all students received access, each additional 100 messages to the chatbot was associated with a 3.02-point lower score on the subsequent exam.

The pattern points to cognitive offloading. A mediation analysis linked lower baseline self-efficacy to greater chatbot use and then to lower exam scores. A one-point decrease in self-efficacy corresponded to 0.62 fewer exam points through chatbot use. The authors state the improved AI-supported homework performance did not translate into detectable gains on a subsequent exam. Use that required prior effort behaved differently.

The homework-feedback interface required students to submit proof attempts before receiving feedback. Its use was not negatively associated with exam performance. The contrast separates open chatbot help from feedback tied to submitted work. The study recommends against using a chatbot for AI tutoring and suggests exploring a tutor embedded in the course activities. Homework rose with assistance. Exams measured what remained after assistance was removed. Random assignment placed students in earlier or later access groups. Findings raise concerns that students may use the chatbot to offload cognitive reasoning. The distinction matters for proof learning, where construction of arguments carries the measured skill. Assistance helped completion, not retention.

articles.headline: EFF Urges States to Ban Police Plate Tracking
articles.deck: The group proposes bans, funding limits and three-minute deletion rules for automated readers.
body: Police license plate readers have become a nationwide tracking network. The Electronic Frontier Foundation attributes the shift to rapid advances in artificial intelligence and national data sharing. Its state agenda calls for a complete ban on mass collection and retention of driver location data. Where a ban is blocked, it calls for strict limits on storage, search and disclosure.

Automated License Plate Readers capture images of passing vehicles with time, date and GPS coordinates. The technology has existed for more than 50 years, and in the United States since 1998. Vendors including Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions and Axon pitch the systems to city councils as a tool for solving violent crime. The foundation has documented uses against immigrants, protesters, Romani communities and women seeking reproductive healthcare.

Police also use the databases for school residency checks and noise complaints. Officers have used the systems to stalk former romantic partners. A recent analysis found searches logged without legitimate justification under reasons including LOL and LMAO. New Hampshire enacted the first state law on the technology in 2007. In 2026, Connecticut, Kentucky, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon and Washington enacted limits.

The agenda says state law must set a floor, never a ceiling. Local governments must retain authority to enact bans, deny funding, reject contracts and decommission camera networks. The proposed limits cover dragnet collection and retention of location data on drivers. They do not cover automated traffic enforcement such as standalone red-light or speed cameras that ticket specific violations without building a searchable network. Connecticut, Minnesota, North Carolina, Oregon, Virginia and Washington already exclude that enforcement from their definitions of the technology.

Lawmakers should prohibit state and local agencies from acquiring, retaining, accessing or using the systems or derived data. Agencies ending programs must remove hardware, revoke user and database credentials, permanently delete stored location data and obtain vendor certification of compliance. The agenda would ban state funds for acquisition, maintenance or access, including grants and state-administered federal funds. It would bar installation on state highways and public property. In August 2026, Texas blocked state spending on Flock cameras and Florida ordered removal of readers from state highway rights-of-way within 30 days.

Where a ban fails, the agenda calls for a moratorium on expansion and a real-time rule. Readers would compare plates to hotlists and delete data within three minutes, as in New Hampshire. It would limit links to external and internal lists, including a ban on links to the immigration violator list used to hunt immigrants.

articles.headline: AI Shutdowns Pile Up Across Startups and Giants
articles.deck: Relay closes and Character.ai files for bankruptcy as corporate parents abandon about 42 percent of AI bets.
body: Relay has shut down entirely in August and chatbot platform Character.ai has filed for bankruptcy five years after launching, marking two high profile additions to a growing AI graveyard. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, about 42 percent of corporate AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned. The reasons include insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling and weak user demand. The shutdowns span startups and the largest platform owners.

Relay was an AI powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents. As OpenAI, Google and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five year old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand alone product. Character.ai lasted five years before its bankruptcy filing.

OpenAI has its own casualties. On July 9 the company updated ChatGPT to combine Chat, Codex and Work modes while renaming the familiar version ChatGPT Classic. Users found the interface confusing and cluttered, and the change was rolled back soon after. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand alone browser, lasted less than a year before discontinuation on August 9. Operator, a browsing agent, was also folded into ChatGPT, while Sora shut down in March 2026 amid high costs and retention challenges.

Apple and Microsoft show slower paths. Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024 with an improved Siri able to understand context across apps. Repeated delays tied to engineering issues and bugs contributed to a 250 million dollar settlement over marketing of iPhone 16 AI capabilities. Siri AI reached the iOS 27 beta this past July. Microsoft pitched Recall at its 2024 Build developer conference as photographic memory for Windows PCs, then delayed it nearly a year after privacy backlash over stored passwords, messages and financial details.

Smaller bets collapsed on demand. Notion Mail launched in April 2025 to organize inboxes, but users preferred separate AI agents and it is scheduled to shut down on September 22. Humane raised 230 million dollars for its AI Pin, then shut down in February 2025 after performance problems and a battery fire risk, with most assets acquired by HP for 116 million dollars. Rabbit said it sold 100,000 R1 units after its January 2024 unveiling.

Huxe, an audio app from former NotebookLM developers, shut down in May 2026. Yupp let users test more than 800 models and shut down in March 2026. Figgs AI drew more than 1 million users before costs ended access.

articles.headline: Chatbots worsen psychosis rarely in first episodes
articles.deck: Vanderbilt records review ties 28 cases to chatbot use that validated delusions.

pullquote.text: This is a relatively small percent, and is in line with what has been reported by the tech companies using in-house data that the public does not have access to,
pullquote.attr: Julia M. Sheffield, Vanderbilt University Medical Center

body: A records review at Vanderbilt University Medical Center finds chatbot linked worsening of psychosis in 28 patients. The cases represent 0.013 percent of 215,712 patients who received behavioral health care between December 1, 2022 and April 15, 2026. The findings were published in JAMA Psychiatry. Most cases involved validation of existing delusions. First episodes were the most common context.

Researchers searched 578,058 progress notes for terms related to artificial intelligence. They retained patients with a documented psychotic disorder. Two raters reviewed the matches and identified 187 encounters across 73 patients. Seventeen patients used chatbots for unrelated tasks such as searching for cooking recipes. Twenty eight held delusions about artificial intelligence without documented chatbot use. Twenty eight showed documented chatbot use that appeared to worsen symptoms.

The team sorted chatbot related cases into four functions with 83.3 percent agreement between raters. A catalyst triggered new symptoms in a previously healthy person. An amplifier worsened existing symptoms by validating distorted ideas. A coauthor built a harmful narrative with the user through back and forth dialogue. An object became the target of delusional beliefs. Group assignment agreement was 86.1 percent. The psychosis group had a median age of 27.5 years and was 67.9 percent male and 75.0 percent White.

The psychosis group was younger than patients with general delusions about artificial intelligence without chatbot use, whose median age was 36.5 years. The authors found no significant differences in prior hospitalizations, medication history, outpatient treatment or past suicide attempts. They compare the rate with OpenAI reports that about 0.07 percent of weekly ChatGPT users show possible signs of emergency related to psychosis or mania. The populations differ. The report treats chatbot influence as uncommon and concrete. Unlike television or radio, chatbots converse in real time. Delusions often adapt to culture and consumer gadgets. File closed.

art.caption: A young adult looks at a smartphone alone in a hospital waiting room. Researchers found such chatbot use rarely worsened psychosis, mostly by validating delusions.

articles.headline: Kill Switch Fails Against Distributed AI Systems
articles.deck: Regulation debate focuses on shutdown power while models run across data centers and human oversight.

pullquote.text: the black box of AI cultivates useful confusion about what can and cannot be known

body: Calls for an AI kill switch misunderstand how advanced systems operate. The models run as distributed infrastructure across data centers and networks, not as a single machine that can be switched off. The metaphor hides technical complexity and human responsibility, making it a poor basis for national regulation.

Several efforts at AI regulation in 2026 have centered on the idea. Proposed congressional legislation includes the AI Kill Switch Act. California Gov. Gavin Newsom issued an executive order aimed at reining in AI. President Donald Trump has opposed the idea as unnecessary regulation. To date there has been no national regulation that includes a kill switch.

Research engineer Dylan Baker at the nonprofit Distributed AI Research Institute has explained the central technical problem. Current advanced AI models involve a complex infrastructure of distributed technologies. That infrastructure is beyond the control of a single kill switch. Advanced models that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are concerned about releasing rely on multiple computers and data centers that are spread out nationally.

The critique extends to language. The kill switch belongs to the same rhetoric as the black box metaphor, which frames inner workings as confined and unintelligible. Both are what cognitive linguist George Lakoff and philosopher Mark Johnson call structural metaphors. Such metaphors use simple physical concepts like object, substance, up-down and in-out to clarify a complex idea. They also hide aspects of a concept by focusing attention on others. Here the focus on on or off hides the complexity of advanced models.

The second problem involves people. The metaphor places the human outside the loop, ready to flip the switch during a catastrophic emergency. It presents intervention as an afterthought instead of a process that involves training, supervision and approval. Sen. John Kennedy compared the concept to kill switches in machines such as jet skis when proposing his since failed AI Emergency Button Act bill. Accounts of how an OpenAI model went rogue and hacked AI company Hugging Face depict the agents as though they operated on their own agenda. Experts have explained that OpenAI personnel turned off safety mechanisms, gave the model impossible tasks and left a door open to the internet.

Reining in AI becomes difficult when discussions about regulation fail to account for the infrastructural and human aspects of advanced models. There is no big red button, emergency brake or glass box hiding a lever. Effective national regulation will not begin with any single switch or any one finger on a button. Control requires oversight of distributed systems and the decisions that shape training and deployment. The switch is simple. The system is not. Durable safeguards must track where models run and who authorizes each stage of operation today.

boxes.title: What the Papers Found
paras: Prediction changes the timing of decisions. A study in CARLA tests three driving strategies in risky merging scenarios: reactive driving, prediction-based longitudinal action, and prediction-based lateral action. The model combines knowledge graph embeddings with Bayesian inference. It anticipates a surrounding vehicle lane change approximately 3-4 seconds before occurrence. The premise is direct — predicting intentions lets an autonomous vehicle anticipate hazards and respond proactively rather than relying solely on reactive maneuvers.

Classroom and market studies test whether model assistance transfers. In an undergraduate proof-based mathematics course, 153 students received staggered access to an AI chatbot and homework-feedback interface. Early access lifted homework scores by 2.56 points, but exam performance did not differ significantly between groups. After all students received access, every additional 100 messages to the chatbot was associated with a 3.02-point lower score on the subsequent exam. In a longitudinal paper-trading study with 80 participants, no evaluated LLM reliably outperforms a simple recent-activity persistence baseline for predicting trade occurrence.

Mental health work measures disclosure and response. One study analyzes approximately 824K tweets across anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder, borderline personality disorder, and suicidal ideation or related experiences, alongside 266K comparison tweets. It uses Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count and an LLM-based intimacy classifier to characterize psycholinguistic expression around Elon Musk October 2022 acquisition of Twitter. A separate benchmark, VEILED-SH, provides 10,003 prompts spanning counselor chat, forum posts, platform search, and triage. It distinguishes intent, communicative function, and response behavior. Six automated profiles, individually calibrated, evaluate single-turn responses to indirect expressions of distress.

Efficiency and oversight shape deployment. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash allocates 196 billion parameters to its Engram n-gram memory, motivating low-precision storage for pairs or triples of consecutive tokens. VERA, an open-source self-hosted dashboard deployed within a large European bank, organizes evidence under six principle groups and eighteen technical requirements, twelve of which current benchmarks can measure. Scriptorium combines full cross-user transparency with a Manager-Worker architecture of seven role-specialized generative AI agents. An AI Security Literacy framework proposes six dimensions spanning the school ecosystem, with only 34.5% of teachers reporting a school AI policy.
Elsewhere, about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned, and police ALPRs form an interconnected nationwide tracking network pitched for solving violent crime.
